content: New treatment regimens are being implemented. Similar to cross-sectional reports, cohort reports can be broken down by sex, age, and pregnancy or breastfeeding status to assess how different populations are progressing on treatment. For instance, this analysis can determine whether men are more likely to be lost to follow-up (LTFU) compared to women or whether younger adults are alive and on antiretroviral therapy (ART) at different time points compared to older adults. Both cross-sectional and cohort reports rely on the ART register as their primary data source. While cohort analysis reports are conceptually more complex, they are easier to compile in practice because they consolidate data into a single column (e.g., month 12) for all cohorts in the register. In contrast, cross-sectional reports require data to be tallied across multiple columns depending on when patients started ART. For example, in a December 2021 report, December 2021 might represent baseline (month 0) for some cohorts, month 5 for those starting in July 2021, or month 9 for those starting in March 2021. Web Annex L provides a generic HIV cross-sectional report, while Web Annex M offers an example of an ART cohort report. Updates to ART attrition data include changes to the timing of viral load (VL) testing based on the World Health Organization (WHO) VL monitoring algorithm and variations in reporting frequency (monthly at subnational levels and quarterly at national levels). In cohort reports, LTFU is defined as 28 days or more since a missed appointment, including missed antiretroviral (ARV) refills in either facility or community settings. These reports also incorporate updates to VL testing timing per WHO recommendations and include key clinical outcomes such as VL suppression and retention on ART at 12, 24, and 36 months. WHO-recommended tools for HIV patient monitoring include appointment books in health facilities for tracking missed visits or drug pickups and pharmacy records to monitor adherence. Key data elements for pharmacy records include the date of ARV pickup, the number of days for which ARVs were dispensed, and the ARV regimen dispensed. Community-based ART patient monitoring tools, as outlined in the 2021 WHO differentiated service delivery (DSD) guidelines, allow clients to initiate ART outside health facilities and reduce the frequency of clinical visits and medication pickups for those established on ART. These services can be accessed at decentralized points, including community-based services. To manage the increasing number of people enrolled in HIV care programs, WHO recommends task-shifting, enabling clinical settings to focus on individuals initiating treatment or those who are unwell, while delegating the monitoring of stable ART patients to supervised lay providers. Community ART service providers play a critical role by linking clients to health facility services (e.g., HIV testing, counseling, and treatment), distributing medications to clients in their homes or communities, providing psychosocial and adherence support, and connecting clients with community-based support groups. Given the wide range of activities performed by community health workers and service providers, it is essential that they routinely monitor and report on a standardized set of actions in a simple and consistent manner. Patient monitoring is vital for linking community and facility health workers and supporting DSD. This reconciliation should occur monthly or quarterly during facility meetings. If community health workers distribute ARVs, their records should also align with pharmacy dispensing records. The new community ART monitoring tool includes a generic community-based patient monitoring framework for DSD ART services, designed for use by community health workers providing HIV care outside health facilities. This tool emphasizes the importance of routine monitoring and reporting on a standardized set of actions. Recommended data elements for community DSD ART data collection include ART initiation site, referral facility details, community ART group number (if applicable), unique identifiers, patient demographics (e.g., name, sex, date of birth, address), visit dates, ART initiation date, ARV regimen details, TB symptoms, missed ARV doses, reasons for non-adherence, and other clinical issues. It also tracks transfers, deaths, treatment interruptions, and pregnancy status. Integration and linkage of HIV services with other health services are crucial for comprehensive patient management. Accurate data collection and reporting are essential for achieving the UN Political Declaration's 95–95–95 targets for HIV treatment and care. DQAs evaluate data accuracy, reliability, completeness, timeliness, accessibility, relevance, and confidentiality. These assessments should be routine and integrated into health information systems to address systemic issues affecting data quality. Efforts to improve data quality should include training, supportive supervision, and mentoring for health care workers and data clerks. Smart design of patient monitoring tools can enhance data quality and reduce the time spent on reporting tasks. Data quality improvement (DQI) strategies should address underlying issues contributing to data quality challenges and link assessments with corrective actions. For example, errors identified in data should be corrected at the point of service delivery. Standardized information products, such as dashboards and performance reports, can facilitate data use for improved patient management and service delivery. Enhanced data analysis and use can identify gaps in service delivery, improve program management, and inform policy decisions. Regular feedback to data custodians and users is critical for improving data quality and utilization. Health care providers should have opportunities to review and discuss collected data, supported by tools like dashboards and standardized information products. Training and mentorship programs should equip data users with the skills to analyze and interpret data effectively. Supportive supervision, including regular site visits and district-level meetings, can foster accountability and the sharing of best practices. WHO, UNAIDS, PEPFAR, and The Global Fund have developed joint DQA tools to harmonize approaches for reviewing and validating HIV patient monitoring data. These tools include checks for data completeness, consistency, and accuracy, as well as supportive actions to strengthen HIV patient monitoring systems. Routine DQAs should target key HIV indicators, such as ART coverage and VL suppression, to improve service quality and treatment outcomes. Data use at the point of collection enhances clinical care, strengthens health services, and improves data quality.
